turns.content: In one observational experiment, P(A)=0.7, P(B)=0.3, and P(A intersect B)=0.2. The quantity of interest is the probability of A after learning that the outcome belongs to B. Explain in words what restricting attention to outcomes in B means.
Treat membership in B as the cause of the lower conditional probability of A and state that this B-to-A causal direction is identified by the observational probabilities.
Write 'the probability of A given B' in standard conditional-probability notation, keeping the conditioning direction explicit.
Assuming P(B)>0, write the formula for that conditional probability in terms of the intersection and the conditioning event.
Substitute P(A intersect B)=0.2 and P(B)=0.3 into the formula, but leave the resulting ratio unsimplified.
Evaluate the ratio and compare the conditional probability P(A given B) with the marginal probability P(A)=0.7.
Check the result by partitioning B into A intersect B and its complement within B. Does the calculation satisfy the probability bounds and use the intended conditioning direction?
State the final conditional probability and give one concise interpretation for the original observational population, without making a causal claim.
